title: Hidden treasures
hookLine: Nyingma teachings said to be hidden and later found by treasure-revealers

lines: A SMALL BOX, A YELLOW SCROLL.
cards: A rider stops at the foot of a cliff in eastern Tibet. He has seen this place before, he says, in a dream. He climbs to a crack in the rock, reaches in, and draws out a small box.

Inside is a roll of yellow paper covered in signs no one around him can read. He wraps it carefully and tells almost nobody. Months later, maybe years, he sits down and begins to write out a whole teaching from it.
That, in the Nyingma telling, is how a hidden treasure comes to light. Today: hidden treasures.

teach.b: First, the word, which you met in year three, in Tibet's dark years. Terma means treasure, and in the Nyingma school it names teachings hidden on purpose, to be found later.

Tradition says Padmasambhava and his close disciple Yeshe Tsogyal hid many teachings across Tibet, because the people then weren't ready for them; they were meant for a later age that would need them.
Second, where treasures hide. Some are earth treasures, sealed in rocks, lakes, statues or pillars, like the box in the cliff.

Others are mind treasures, hidden, the tradition says, in the deep mind of a disciple, to rise up whole in a later life. The scrolls are often said to be written in a coded script that only one person can read.
Third, the treasure-revealer, called a terton. Tradition says a terton is a disciple of Padmasambhava reborn, with a seal on the mind that opens at the right time and place.
Revealing a treasure isn't treated as easy or safe: a terton may wait for signs, keep the find secret, and check it with other teachers.
Fourth, what came out of the ground.
Tradition holds that the text often called the Tibetan Book of the Dead, read aloud to the dying, which you met in year one as the bardo teachings, is a treasure revealed this way.
Some readers take terma as literal finds, some as visionary revelation, some as both. What the Nyingma stress is the idea underneath: teaching that waits until someone needs it.

how: Nyingma Buddhists practice from terma, treasure teachings said to have been hidden by Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal and revealed later by tertons, alongside the teachings passed down without interruption from teacher to student.

games.q: you're a terton. you've just pulled a yellow scroll from a crack in a cliff you saw in a dream. what do you do?
o: read it aloud in the village square tonight.
keep it quiet, wait for the right time, and check it with teachers.
put it back; it's too strange.
games.why: in the Nyingma telling, a terton often waits, keeps the find secret, and checks it before writing out the teaching.

practice: Let one old teaching of your own surface, a line from earlier on this path or something a grandparent said, that you'd half forgotten.

Maybe the Dhammapada's opening, in Max Müller's words: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." Turn it over once, the way a terton might unroll a scroll, then hold it quietly, as if it had waited for today.

wordCard.voice: Terma. Treasure: Nyingma teachings said to be hidden by Padmasambhava and Yeshe Tsogyal and found later by treasure-revealers called tertons. Today's word.

orig.note: Tibetan: terma, treasure. a terton (གཏེར་སྟོན) is one who reveals treasure.

carryVoice: Your line: hidden treasure. Some teaching waits until it's needed. Rest well.
